sources.text: A process sleeps in order to wait for a condition to become true, and the chan argument (the wait channel) names the desired condition. sleep_prepare(chan) declares that a process might soon sleep in order to wait for the indicated wait channel; it returns right away. wakeup(chan) is called when the condition named by chan has (or might have) become true; it wakes up all processes that have called sleep_prepare(chan) and then sleep() with the same chan. sleep() returns right away if wakeup(chan) has already been called after the (required) previous call to sleep_prepare(chan); if not, sleep() marks the calling process as SLEEPING (not RUNNABLE) and releases the CPU by context-switching to the scheduler, so that other processes can run. sleep_prepare() and sleep() are called by the same process (typically within a few lines of each other); wakeup() is called by a different process or by an interrupt handler.

sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.

questions.stem:
A producer-consumer buffer uses the xv6-style wait protocol. A consumer C holds the condition lock L while checking the condition, and a producer P calls wakeup(chan) for the shared wait channel chan.

Conditions:
1. sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns; it may be called before checking the condition or before releasing the lock that protects the condition.
2. If wakeup(chan) runs after sleep_prepare(chan) but before sleep() acquires p->lock, wakeup(chan) sees p->chan == chan and sets p->chan to zero.
3. If wakeup(chan) runs after sleep() has marked the process SLEEPING, wakeup(chan) sees that state and marks the process RUNNABLE.
4. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() marks the caller SLEEPING and calls sched().
5. A process must release the condition lock before sleep() and re-acquire it after sleep() returns.
6. In the consumer, the condition is "buffer non-empty"; in the producer, the condition is "buffer non-full". Both use the same chan.

Question: Which rewrite of the consumer is correct, and why?
options: Consumer variant 1: check "buffer non-empty" while holding L; if empty, call sleep_prepare(chan); release L; call sleep(); re-acquire L; then recheck "buffer non-empty" before deciding whether to retry. This is correct because sleep_prepare(chan) is ordered before releasing L, so a wakeup cannot be lost, and the condition is rechecked after re-acquiring L to handle any state change during the sleep.

Consumer variant 2: release L; call sleep_prepare(chan); check "buffer non-empty"; if empty, call sleep(); re-acquire L. This is correct because the consumer holds no lock while sleeping, so wakeup always runs after sleep_prepare and is never lost.

Consumer variant 3: check "buffer non-empty" while holding L; if empty, call sleep(); then release L; after sleep() returns, re-acquire L. This is correct because sleep() itself atomically releases L and marks the process SLEEPING.

Consumer variant 4: call sleep_prepare(chan) once at startup; later, without holding L, check "buffer non-empty" and call sleep() if empty; wakeup(chan) will always be seen because p->chan is permanently non-zero.
questions.explanation:
A is correct: sleep_prepare must happen before checking the condition or before releasing the lock protecting the condition; otherwise wakeup can run before p->chan is set and be lost. After the lock is re-acquired, the condition must be rechecked because the buffer state may have changed while the process slept.

Variant 2 is wrong because checking the condition after releasing L lets a wakeup happen before sleep_prepare and be lost, and it violates the required ordering of sleep_prepare relative to condition protection.

Variant 3 is wrong because it calls sleep() while still holding L; the lock must be released before sleep() so another process or interrupt can modify the condition and call wakeup().

Variant 4 is wrong because it never rechecks the condition and it does not re-establish the sleep_prepare/sleep ordering for each wait.

It asks the student to evaluate four rewrites against these interacting rules, which requires analysis of a lost-wakeup scenario rather than recalling a definition.

expected_steps: Recognize that sleep_prepare(chan) must be called before checking the condition or before releasing the condition lock.
Identify that wakeup between sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep() sets p->chan to zero so sleep() returns without sleeping.
Check that the consumer releases L before sleep() and re-acquires L after it returns.
Require rechecking the condition after re-acquiring L because the buffer state may have changed during the sleep.
Reject variants that check the condition without protection, call sleep() while still holding L, or never recheck the condition.

It then releases L and calls sleep(); sleep() returns immediately if p->chan was zeroed by wakeup, otherwise it marks itself SLEEPING and yields. After sleep() returns it must re-acquire L and recheck the condition, because the condition may have changed or another consumer may have consumed the item. A producer-consumer buffer uses the xv6-style wait protocol. A consumer C holds the condition lock L while checking the condition, and a producer P calls wakeup(chan) for the shared wait channel chan.

1. sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns; it may be called before checking the condition or before releasing the lock that protects the condition.
2. If wakeup(chan) runs after sleep_prepare(chan) but before sleep() acquires p->lock, wakeup(chan) sees p->chan == chan and sets p->chan to zero.
3. If wakeup(chan) runs after sleep() has marked the process SLEEPING, wakeup(chan) sees that state and marks the process RUNNABLE.
4. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() marks the caller SLEEPING and calls sched().
5. A process must release the condition lock before sleep() and re-acquire it after sleep() returns.
6. In the consumer, the condition is "buffer non-empty"; in the producer, the condition is "buffer non-full". Both use the same chan.

Question: Which rewrite of the consumer is correct, and why?

A pipe reader process uses the xv6 sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup interface. The condition lock (a separate lock) protects the condition. The reader wants to sleep when the buffer is empty. Which sequence correctly uses the interface to avoid a lost wakeup?

1. Before checking the condition, the reader must call sleep_prepare(chan).
2. Before calling sleep(), the reader must release the condition lock.
3. After sleep() returns, the reader must re-acquire the condition lock.
4. sleep() must be called after sleep_prepare(chan) and before any wakeup(chan) can occur.
5. If wakeup(chan) occurs after sleep_prepare(chan) but before sleep(), sleep() returns immediately without sleeping.
6. If wakeup(chan) occurs before sleep_prepare(chan), sleep() will block forever if the condition never becomes true again.

Which of the following sequences is correct?
options: Call sleep_prepare(chan), check condition, release lock, call sleep(), re-acquire lock after sleep() returns.
Check condition, release lock, call sleep_prepare(chan), call sleep(), re-acquire lock after sleep() returns.
Call sleep_prepare(chan), check condition, call sleep(), release lock after sleep() returns.
Call sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep() while holding the condition lock, then release lock after sleep() returns.

response.evidence_note: All four supplied excerpts describe the sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup protocol, the lost wakeup problem, and the condition lock rules in enough detail to pose one hard MCQ.

questions.stem:
A pipe reader process R waits for a shared buffer that a writer process W fills. R uses the xv6-style wait interface: sleep_prepare(chan), sleep(chan), and wakeup(chan). The condition lock protects the buffer state and prevents wakeup(chan) from being called between R's condition check and R's call to sleep_prepare(chan).

Relevant rules from the course material:
1. sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition.
2. If wakeup(chan) runs between sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup sets a flag indicating the process should not actually sleep; sleep() then returns instead of sleeping.
3. A process must release the condition lock before calling sleep(), so another process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup(); it re-acquires the lock after sleep() returns.
4. Without this protocol, a wakeup() called after R checks the condition but before R calls sleep() would find no sleeping process, so R could sleep forever even though data is available; this is a lost wake-up.
5. After sleep() returns, R must recheck the condition before deciding again whether to sleep.

R is about to run. The buffer is still empty and no wakeup has occurred. Among the following sequences, which one correctly protects R against a lost wake-up while keeping the required lock behavior?

A. R calls sleep_prepare(chan); acquires the condition lock; checks the condition (buffer empty, so R must wait); releases the condition lock; calls sleep(chan); after sleep returns, re-acquires the condition lock and rechecks the condition.

B. R acquires the condition lock; checks the condition (buffer empty, so R must wait); releases the condition lock; calls sleep_prepare(chan); calls sleep(chan); after sleep returns, re-acquires the condition lock and rechecks the condition.

C. R acquires the condition lock; checks the condition (buffer empty); calls sleep_prepare(chan); calls sleep(chan) while still holding the condition lock; after sleep returns, rechecks the condition without releasing the lock.

D. R acquires the condition lock; checks the condition (buffer empty); calls sleep(chan) directly without sleep_prepare(chan); after sleep returns, re-acquires the condition lock and rechecks the condition.

questions.explanation:
Option A follows both required rules: sleep_prepare(chan) is called before checking the condition (rule 1), and the condition lock is held during the check, released before sleep(chan) (rule 3), and re-acquired after sleep returns for a condition recheck (rule 5). This guarantees that if W calls wakeup(chan) between R's check and R's sleep(), the flag set by wakeup (rule 2) makes sleep() return immediately, avoiding a lost wake-up (rule 4).

Option B releases the condition lock before calling sleep_prepare(chan). After the check but before sleep_prepare, W could call wakeup(chan) and find p->chan not set; then R would call sleep() and could sleep forever, exactly the lost wake-up in rule 4.

Option C violates rule 3: the condition lock must be released before sleep(), so W or an interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup(); holding the lock during sleep() can prevent wakeup from making progress.

Option D omits sleep_prepare(chan) entirely, so wakeup cannot set the no-sleep flag before sleep(), and a wakeup arriving between the check and sleep() is lost.

sources.text: A process sleeps in order to wait for a condition to become true, and the chan argument (the wait channel) names the desired condition. sleep_prepare(chan) declares that a process might soon sleep in order to wait for the indicated wait channel; it returns right away. wakeup(chan) is called when the condition named by chan has (or might have) become true; it wakes up all processes that have called sleep_prepare(chan) and then sleep() with the same chan. sleep() returns right away if wakeup(chan) has already been called after the (required) previous call to sleep_prepare(chan); if not, sleep() marks the calling process as SLEEPING (not RUNNABLE) and releases the CPU by context-switching to the scheduler, so that other processes can run. sleep_prepare() and sleep() are called by the same process (typically within a few lines of each other); wakeup() is called by a different process or by an interrupt handler.

sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.
